chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Abi Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

He said: Indeed, Allah, the Exalted, is not a tyrant to His servant, but He tests him with whatever He wills. Among them is one He tests with illness, among them is one He tests with poverty, among them is one He tests with death, among them is one He tests with hunger and thirst, among them is one He tests with drought, among them is one He tests with defeat, among them is one He tests with wealth, among them is one He tests with poverty, among them is one He tests with illness, among them is one He tests with health, among them is one He tests with beauty, among them is one He tests with ugliness, among them is one He tests with knowledge, among them is one He tests with ignorance, among them is one He tests with strength, among them is one He tests with weakness, among them is one He tests with wealth, among them is one He tests with poverty. So whoever is patient, he triumphs, and whoever is patient, he triumphs, and whoever is patient, he triumphs.

key_terms.ظَلَّامٍ: Tyrant or one who deals unjustly

ai.seo_question: What are the different types of divine tests mentioned in Shia hadith and how does patience lead to triumph?
ai.summary: In *Kamal al-Din*, Shaykh al-Saduq records Imam al-Sadiq’s (a) clarification that divine trials (balā’) are not acts of oppression but necessary tests to distinguish the steadfast from the negligent. This narration underscores the Shia theological principle that patience (sabr) is the active mechanism for spiritual elevation, transforming worldly hardships into means of attaining divine proximity and ultimate victory.
